title: Show HN: Shh-code – coding agent with privacy
story_key: story|title:shh code coding agent with privacy
content_excerpt: Anyone who thinks for themselves needs a safe place to think out loud: to turn over a personal question, work an idea through before it's ready, or build something that is their own. Done in a chat with a model, that thinking leaves a record on someone else's servers, where the provider may use it or train on it, and where a breach could hand your history to people who would use it against you. shh, short for Sovereign Human Headspace, exists so that your thinking can happen without leaving that record in readable form on anyone's servers: your prompts go only to an enclave the provider can't read, and shh checks that before it sends anything. shh-code can do most of what other coding agents do, but privately. It works in your terminal, reads, writes and edits files, runs shell commands and searches the web, and asks you before it changes or runs anything; shh-code chat turns it into a general assistant. What sets it apart is where your prompts go. It only talks to models running in attested, end-to-end encrypted confidential-computing enclaves (TEEs) on Tinfoil , and it refuses to send anything when it can't verify the enclave. There is no fallback to a plaintext or unattested path. Experimental software. shh-code is provided AS IS, without warranty of any kind, and you use it at your own risk. It is not meant for production use, or for code and data you can't afford to expose. It has not had an independent security audit: the only reviews so far were done by a coding agent. See LICENSE-MIT and LICENSE-APACHE for the terms, and SECURITY.md for what it protects and where it falls short. We recommend running it inside a sandbox of its own, such as a VM, a container or an agent sandbox tool; docs/network.md lists the hosts it needs there. You need Python 3.11 or newer on macOS 13+ or Linux, and a Tinfoil API key. On Linux, also install bubblewrap for the Bash sandbox ( sudo apt install bubblewrap on Debian or Ubuntu). title: Hill-climbing Inkling 2 Mini inference on one RTX PRO 6000
story_key: story|variant:mini,pro|title:hill climbing inkling 2 mini inference on one rtx pro 6000
content_excerpt: Inkling 2 Mini came out last week and sets a new state of the art for local AI and smaller open-source models. With ~26B total parameters (3B active per token), multimodal inputs, and a 1M-token context window, it leads its weight class on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 and across 32 of 48 benchmarks against models like Gemma 4 31B and Qwen3.8-27B, making it a strong open option for coding, tool use, and reasoning on modest hardware. We wrote an extensive blog post on how you can use it within the Hugging Face ecosystem here . One of the interesting aspects of Inkling 2 Mini that might explain its great performance is its unusual architecture. Inkling 2 Mini is a looped Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model with 24 physical layers where the middle 12 layers run three times, so every token passes through 48 layers. The checkpoint ships in mixed NVFP4 and MXFP8 and bundles a DSpark drafter for speculative decoding. Both vLLM and SGLang, the go-to frameworks for LLM inference, support it on nightly builds, though the published serving recipes target NVIDIA B200 and GB300 GPUs ( sm100 ), leaving out sm120 cards like the NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 where kernel compatibility can differ. We wanted to see how fast we could serve it on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 96 GB, the GPU behind an nvidia-rtx-pro-6000 Inference Endpoint . Rather than tuning flags by hand, we gave a coding agent the inference-optimisation skill, the hf CLI, and access to Hugging Face Jobs , and let it run experiments for an afternoon. Across 46 valid benchmark runs, single-user decode went from 136 to 190.6 tok/s (+40%) (ahead of the 167.7 tok/s community SGLang + DSpark benchmark on LocalMaxxing for the same GPU) and 8-user aggregate throughput went from ~570 to 716 tok/s (+26%) using vLLM nightly with DSpark speculative decoding. Greedy outputs are byte-identical with and without speculation, long-context needle retrieval passes 3/3 up to 250K tokens, and the winning config is now running as an Inference Endpoint from a pinned image digest. All logs, scripts, and raw measurements are in NielsRogge/inkling-2-mini-hillclimb . The inference-optimisation skill gives an agent a fixed experimental protocol and a small, engine-agnostic benchmark script ( bench.py ): bench.py measures single-user decode, aggregate decode at concurrency N, cold prefill at several lengths, and TTFT, using token counts directly from the server's usage response. title: Show HN: Fork Linux desktops in 139ms for computer-use agent training
story_key: story|title:fork linux desktops in 139ms for computer use agent training
content_excerpt: Host daemon for the Drums shared runtime: many isolated Linux desktops per server, with CRIU restore, fork and reset, for computer-use RL The host daemon of the Drums shared runtime: hundreds of isolated Linux desktops on one server, restored from CRIU checkpoints, forked and reset without a reboot, with a gate report and a reward audit on every episode. Training a computer-use agent needs thousands of isolated desktops, and the usual answer is one virtual machine per desktop, each booting its own kernel, operating system and applications. Drums takes a different route: one Linux host runs one booted desktop image, and every environment is a private copy-on-write state on top of it (its own overlay root, its own pid, mount, network, ipc, uts and user namespaces, its own cgroup). An environment is not booted; it is restored from a CRIU checkpoint of a running desktop, so a reset or a fork brings up Chrome, LibreOffice or GIMP where they were, in seconds, and many environments share the image's pages. drumsd is the daemon that owns those environments on a host. It creates, resets, saves (captures), forks (branches), quarantines and destroys them; drives the Drums fork of CRIU ( drums-criu , one template server per checkpoint); runs every episode behind a set of gates (restore fidelity, isolation, cgroup limits, OOM kills, application crashes) so a trainer never sees a reward from a broken desktop; and audits each reward (a second checker run, a redundant checker, a file-scope scan). It serves an HTTP API on the host that the Python SDK ( drums-sdk ), the Drums gateway and the MCP server talk to. One host serves one tenant. Environments on a host are separated from each other by namespaces, cgroups and per-env uid ranges; customers are separated from each other by virtual machines. See Security . A fresh Ubuntu 24.04 x86_64 machine with cgroup v2 (the default), 16 vCPU, 32 GiB of RAM and a 150 GiB disk, with outbound HTTPS during the install. Every release is tested on an AWS c8i.4xlarge. A release is one self-contained tarball, drums-release-<commit>.tar.gz , from the releases page . Every input it needs (apt snapshot, the OSWorld image, the drums-criu and SDK commits, the Rust toolchain, a hashed Python lock) is pinned in install/lock.json and verified; the first mismatch stops the install. title: Migrating our Messages API to Rust
summary: How we used the existing Messages API to verify the new one, with teams of Claude agents tracking down and fixing differences between the Python and Rust versions.
story_key: story|title:migrating our messages api to rust
content_excerpt: Many problems have a generator–verifier gap: it’s often far easier to verify that a solution is correct than to come up with one. Sudoku is a classic example. It’s simple to check the solution (just count the numbers in each row, column, and box), but finding that solution can take a long time. Many ambitious Claude projects have relied on this gap: formalizing proofs in mathematics or migrating large, well-tested codebases are tasks Claude can take on as long as it has a reliable way to verify its work. But as Claude has become more capable, it’s begun to take on projects in live systems, where generating the work is easier than verifying it. In these systems, users often rely on edge cases and quirks that fall outside the test suite , and it’s hard to write a definition of “correct” that covers everything . Without a reliable way to check Claude’s work, the migration of a live system is hard to trust—however quickly Claude can generate the code for it. We ran into this problem when we migrated our Messages API from Python to Rust. This API is the primary way that customers—as well as our own apps, like Claude Code and Cowork—reach Claude. From early 2024 to fall 2026, API traffic grew roughly 1,800 times. Rust would allow us to use far less CPU per request. Claude wrote a first version of the API’s core request path in about a week. But building trust in the migration required us to find a way to verify that our Rust API was at parity with our production API. This proved hard for several reasons, including that the Python API continued changing throughout the migration, so parity was a moving target; Claude can reply nondeterministically to the same request, so a difference between two outputs didn’t necessarily mean a bug; and we couldn't read customer requests, so we weren't able to easily see where the two versions diverged. In this post, we share how we turned the production Messages API itself into a verifier—and how that helped us test the new Rust version on production traffic, find where it differed, and automatically dispatch agents to fix those differences. This allowed us to ship an API on Rust that uses about 70% less CPU per request and cuts median time to first token by about 20% without ever taking the service offline or freezing feature development. title: An $80K breach forced us to own our AI stack. We're never going back
story_key: story|title:an 80k breach forced us to own our ai stack we re never going back
content_excerpt: How last month's Railway incident made us rethink what infrastructure has become table stakes for AI-native companies The TLDR: Over the past month, we moved almost all of Dreamwork's backend onto servers and cloud accounts we control - deploying our own fine-tuned models in charge of applying, custom classifier models for our data filtering + enrichment, and rolling out a custom lightweight browser built specifically for crawling nearly 3M live jobs across ~140,000 companies. The result is higher reliability, faster iteration, and dramatically lower operating costs...and it made us rethink some things in the process. To understand why we made such a drastic change, we need to go back to Railway's security incident on Oct 20. Per their incident report, an attacker decrypted environment variables for a subset of workspaces and went after AI provider keys. As a result of this, several of our keys were exposed and abused immediately, running up $80K+ in unauthorized inference before we were even notified. While dealing with the fallout, we took this as a clear signal to stop renting the core of our stack. As AI models become more capable, these kinds of security incidents are only going to get worse. And security isn't the only reason to own inference anymore. Data visibility and unit economics have become just as important. Applying to jobs across thousands of different employer portals is an inherently messy, stateful problem. Deterministic rules or narrow structured decision models break the moment a site changes a widget, throws a custom validation error, or shifts its multi-step flow. title: Can a Frontier LLM Repair a Quantized Network by Tool-Free Weight-Space Programming?
summary: We give four large language models (LLMs) of the Claude family the complete weights of a 20k-parameter CIFAR-10 CNN as text and ask them to produce a 4-bit network without tools, data or the ability to run inference. Standard round-to-nearest (RTN) quantization to 4 bit lowers the test accuracy from 81.4% to 60.4%. We design four evaluation protocols that differ in the input and task description given to the LLMs and analyze their responses. In the first two protocols the LLMs are given the float and the 4-bit RTN network and are told that the accuracy has dropped significantly. In the last two they receive only the float network and the task to quantize it, which tests whether they apply an optimization on their own or fall back to plain RTN. Our analysis shows that a frontier LLM can recover most of the lost accuracy. Given one answer per layer, Opus 5.5 raises the accuracy of the 4-bit network to 77.95% by balancing the rounding errors within each 3x3 kernel, reasoning over the integer weights without tools. This is 3.5 pp below the float network and 2.8 pp below AdaRound, which learns the rounding from calibration data. Given only the float network, the LLMs name error-cancelling corrections but do not apply them and fall back to plain RTN, at most with mildly clipped scales, which still lifts Fable 5.2's quantized network to 70.0%. We analyze in detail what the LLMs did and why it works. Code and prompts can be found at https://github.com/urbste/weight-space-programming-ptq

title: Worth the Wait? How Response Time and Streaming Shape Judgments of Generative AI Answers and Chatbot Engagement
summary: Answers from generative AI chatbots built on large language models (LLMs) now arrive at very different speeds: reasoning models deliberate before replying, while response caches can return a stored answer at once. Blind preference votes, which rank these models, are read as judgments of their text, and if delivery matters, faster answers are expected to gain. Research on the labor illusion and on how text appears on screen suggests instead that an answer which unfolds as it is written is credited over the same answer shown at once. We test these accounts with three sources of variation in natural use. First, compar:IA, a French government chatbot arena, answered repeated prompts, by a random draw, either with a fresh answer streamed as it was written or with a stored earlier answer from the same model, shown at once. Within the same prompt, a replay lowered an answer's chance of winning a decisive blind vote by 25.8 percentage points. The same stored text won 57% of its decisive votes when streamed and 29% when replayed, and voters called it less complete, more superficial and more often incorrect when replayed. Second, provider congestion slowed streamed answers. In 324,029 conversations, slower answers earned no detectable net credit in the vote, but a slower first exchange made visitors less likely to ask a follow-up question. Third, in 4,378,514 WildChat replies from everyday ChatGPT use, replies slowed by congestion made users less likely to continue. Delivery moved blind votes, in the direction opposite to the one the arena's designers expected, while waiting cost follow-up questions that a comparison between two answers cannot register when both are slow. The results bear on how AI services cache and stream answers, how they budget latency, and how preference leaderboards evaluate models.

title: Eliciting the Recall Capacity of Linear Attention
summary: Linear attention models exhibit a disproportionate deficit relative to softmax attention in associative recall (AR) in language modeling. We investigate this gap through natural language evaluations, synthetic recall tasks, and targeted training interventions. Using a synthetic setting, we quantify the role of state-size in how many items can be recalled from memory and find a similar empirical scaling across the tested linear-attention architectures. Testing this relationship reveals that even a single layer at scale can learn to retrieve thousands of associations across long distances. Yet, standard language model training does not reliably teach a linear model to copy from context, whereas a comparable softmax model learns to do so. Considering this, we strengthen recall supervision during training through in-context sentence repetition and context-sensitive loss reweighting. Both methods improve recall-intensive benchmark performance and narrow the long-distance AR gap to the softmax baseline without changing the architecture, token budget, or number of optimization steps, at a slight cost to general language modeling. These targeted changes to training can thus elicit substantial but underutilized retrieval capacity in linear-attention models. These findings suggest that, although linear-attention architectures have substantial capacity for recall, their inductive biases and the demands of language model training make it difficult to develop this capability without dedicated incentives.

  • Press Tab to complete arguments for supported slash commands. For example, /mcp lo completes to /mcp login. (#62343)
  • Jump between task groups in the agent command center with Shift+Up and Shift+Down. (#62200)
  • Optional stdio MCP servers with cached tool lists now start on their first tool call by default. (#62366)
  • Set an approval reviewer for individual connected app tools in config.toml. (#62360)
  • App-server clients can select Amazon Bedrock Runtime during setup or sign-in. (#62222)

Bug Fixes

  • codex exec resume restores saved sandbox permissions, the working directory, and workspace roots unless explicitly overridden. (#62194)
  • Remote sessions preserve working directories, workspace roots, and writable paths when the client and server run on different operating systems. (#62375, #62376, #62377)
  • Codex reports provider errors as soon as they arrive in a response stream and identifies which API spend limit was reached. (#62329, #62356)
  • Interrupting a parent turn preserves queued replies from child agents for the next turn. (#62348)
  • Use PageUp and PageDown to read and submit answer choices that are taller than the terminal’s answer area. (#62209)
  • Cloud replies that finish after history loads now update in place, keeping the terminal transcript in order. (#62403)

Documentation

  • The bundled openai-docs skill now covers migration to GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol, including endpoint choices and tool-calling requirements. (#62447)

Chores

  • Code Mode now uses gRPC for all host connections. The code_mode_host_grpc setting is deprecated. (#62476)
  • Python formatting and SDK type generation now verify dependency hashes against the repository lockfile. (#62346)

title: claude-code v2.1.330
summary:
What's changed

  • Added sign-in to organizations managed in Anthropic's Enterprise Admin Console: after claude auth login, Claude Code applies the organization's settings and uses its cloud provider or gateway
  • Added easel, a built-in mod that draws charts when asked and under MCP metrics results, on Pro, Max and, where available, Team and Enterprise on macOS and Linux; turn automatic charts off in /config
  • Added CLAUDE_CODE_FULL_SIGN_IN_LINK=1 to print the full sign-in link, if the short one shows an error or a script reads values from it
  • Self-hosted runner: Added --start-dir / SELF_HOSTED_RUNNER_START_DIR to have Claude start its work in a folder of a repository, while settings and hooks load as without it
  • Added a notice in cloud and self-hosted runner sessions when a plugin marketplace can't be fetched because its repository isn't one of the session's
  • Self-hosted runner: Added a notice when Anthropic-managed git refuses a plugin's own repository, naming the plugin and what to do
  • Added commandPrinted to claude plugin install --json results, true when the plugin's install command wrote to stderr, and commandFailed when it exited with an error, was killed or timed out
  • Added claude_code_self_hosted_runner_order_to_registered_seconds to the self-hosted runner's /metrics: seconds from work order issued to registration accepted, on orchestrator-spawned runners
  • Added claude_code_self_hosted_runner_order_to_first_session_seconds to the self-hosted runner's /metrics: seconds from work order to first session handed over, on runners started for a session
  • Fixed Claude Code freezing for up to several minutes right after compacting a very long conversation
  • Fixed WebFetch freezing the session for minutes on some pages, and returning an empty result for some others
  • Fixed ExitWorktree and the worktree exit dialog deleting a worktree that another running Claude Code session was working in
  • Fixed changes to user settings being lost when several Claude Code processes saved them at the same time
  • Fixed --continue and --resume opening an empty session or failing when the last saved message had a missing or invalid timestamp
  • Fixed the first prompt after a sleep of two minutes or more waiting three minutes on a connection that had died, on Linux and WSL
  • Fixed turns failing with "JSON schema is invalid", and session files growing by many megabytes, when many MCP tools have an input schema that the API refuses
  • Linux: Fixed Bash commands waiting seconds and showing no file diff for the rest of a session in slow repositories with large ignored folders such as node_modules
  • Windows: Fixed Bash commands running slower for the rest of a session after Git Bash took 10 to 60 seconds to start, on machines with no custom start-up files
  • Fixed /rewind sometimes restoring an older version of a file when two queued prompts, or stacked skills, ran together right after a turn that changed it
  • Fixed text and images added when approving a permission prompt being dropped when the approved command or tool then failed
  • Fixed MCP resources from claude.ai connectors and plugin servers not being attached when @-mentioned in the terminal's prompt box
  • Fixed an MCP server that subagents declare being shut down when one of them finished, while other subagents or the session were still using it
  • Fixed Claude in Chrome staying "not connected" after a brief connection problem, even though Chrome was open and signed in
  • Fixed terminal sessions on Amazon Bedrock (Mantle) started with no model selected ignoring a pinned Opus model, and still calling an unavailable default model after announcing a fallback
  • Fixed the rest of what you were typing being lost when a plan arrived in fullscreen mode
  • Fixed claude.ai connectors with different names being dropped when they share a server URL (#101856)
  • Fixed plugins going missing from the installed list when several claude plugin commands ran at the same time
  • Fixed task dependencies and metadata being lost when several task updates ran at the same time
  • Fixed incomplete backups of ~/.claude.json being kept, and displacing good ones, when the disk was full
  • Fixed a long pause in Code Mode after code that read hundreds of files in projects with path-scoped rules or Read deny rules
  • Fixed the built-in chart tool failing when Claude called it in Code Mode
  • Fixed Code Mode ignoring an MCP tool's request to end the turn from a script in auto and bypass permissions modes
  • Fixed Code Mode in auto mode dropping earlier thinking and rewriting the prompt cache when a mod added a note after a script loaded a skill
  • Fixed Code Mode not restoring a file that a script had read after Esc and /compact
  • Fixed /context undercounting system tools in Code Mode before Claude's first reply
  • Fixed a stopped background subagent sometimes not staying stopped
  • Fixed Claude still waiting for a background agent that was stopped just as it finished, in sessions run by an app or the SDK
  • Fixed background sessions sometimes waking in their previous permission mode after approving a plan
  • Remote Control: Fixed the note about background agents ended by a Stop from a phone or the web showing in the terminal as if you had typed it
  • Remote Control: Fixed the mobile apps hiding the Diff and pull request buttons, or showing a stopped session as working, after turning it on mid-conversation
  • Fixed environment variables written by a SessionStart hook being lost with claude -p --continue
  • Fixed claude -p exiting 0 with no message when its output went to a file on a full disk: it now prints an error and exits 1, though a full NFS export may go unnoticed
  • Fixed the system prompt keeping the earlier model's instructions when the model was changed after /context but before the first message
  • Fixed Claude sometimes replying to its commit attribution reminder and ending the turn early after the model changed mid-turn; it can still happen where managed settings set the PR attribution line
  • Fixed Esc not ending an LSP tool call that was waiting for a slow or stuck language server
  • Fixed LSP tool calls and diagnostics failing when several calls or edits arrived while a language server was still starting
  • Fixed /mcp listing plugin servers as built-in: they now stand under "Plugin MCPs", --mcp-config and built-in servers under "Other MCPs", and a server's page names its plugin
  • Fixed an "MCP server blocked by enterprise policy: easel" warning showing at every start when an MCP allowlist or denylist excludes the built-in chart tool, which stays blocked
  • Fixed /stats counting new activity in UTC days instead of your local time zone
  • Fixed /ultrareview failing or reviewing the wrong code after the shell moved into another repository: it now stops and names both folders
  • Fixed Grep reporting no matches when the pattern held a line break without multiline mode; it now reports the rejected pattern
  • Fixed Jupyter notebooks saved with a byte order mark being reported as invalid JSON by the Read and NotebookEdit tools
  • Fixed link reference definitions being dropped from CLAUDE.md and memory files that contain an HTML comment
  • Fixed running Monitors keeping the earlier conversation in memory until they end
  • Fixed some Claude Desktop sessions on third-party providers, other than scheduled tasks, ending a turn with "Prompt is too long" when a PDF larger than the context window followed a long conversation
  • Fixed the choice between two user or project agent files declaring the same name depending on the order the file search listed them
  • Fixed claude daemon logs never exiting inside a git repository when there is no log file
  • Fixed markdown hiding a character or two after bold or italic text when a backslash came before an emoji later in the paragraph
  • Fixed Edit refusing some valid hook commands in Claude settings files
  • Fixed Read with a page range showing both halves of a scanned two-page spread on each of its pages
  • Fixed line breaks and class stereotypes missing from Mermaid diagrams in HTML artifacts
  • Fixed the Project instructions picker in /config showing only one of its four choices in a 24-row fullscreen window
  • Fixed a subagent's own subagents and forks running on the plan-mode model in plan mode under opusplan or haiku
  • Fixed WebFetch page summaries ignoring the /effort level when a gateway refuses the small fast model
  • Fixed claude -p on Google Cloud's Agent Platform ignoring --settings '{"fastMode":true}' when the model comes from ANTHROPIC_MODEL or a settings file; such runs now bill at the fast mode price
  • Fixed startup under forceLoginOrgUUID being refused after one temporary server error or dropped connection
  • Fixed claude mcp remove giving no way forward for a claude.ai connector: it now says to turn it off in /mcp or remove it on claude.ai
  • Fixed the /mcp "Connect on claude.ai" check saying "not connected" when claude.ai has a connector at the server's URL without its query
  • Fixed /install-github-app and /design-login showing a generic failure for an account on hold instead of the on-hold notice and appeal link
  • Fixed a running MCP task being reported as stopped when you move a session to the background; the background session can now follow the task, but not if its server uses stdio or sets headers
  • Fixed self-hosted runners ignoring a session until they exited, after its failure report was lost or the session was given back to the same runner
  • Fixed self-hosted sessions losing the prompt cache and earlier thinking when the list of repositories a restart couldn't prepare changed
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed tool calls behind a permission prompt vanishing with no result when a new runner took over the prompt, in sessions with telemetry off
  • Fixed resumed self-hosted runner sessions starting without their pushed work in large repositories when --push-outcome-on-release is set
  • Fixed self-hosted runner sessions being shown as working when Claude Code hangs at every start and --startup-timeout-min is from 2 to about 6
  • Fixed pkill -f in self-hosted runner sessions on Linux ending its own shell with exit code 144, or the runner (needs a pkill with --ignore-ancestors)
  • Fixed scheduled tasks on self-hosted runners having no tool to notify their owner when telemetry is off or a third-party provider is used
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed one slow spawn-runner hook keeping the orchestrator from claiming sessions for its free slots; it now polls every 4 to 6 seconds while a slot is free
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed a 403, such as an IP allowlist's, logged as a bad secret or token: most such lines now lead with the server's reason, so update log alerts that match the old words
  • Fixed self-hosted runners' warn mode for repository settings stopping at the first finding of most kinds: it now goes on, up to 50 for a session, and says if it stops early
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed runners that start on a full disk taking sessions and failing them; they now wait for room and exit 1 after a minute with no session, unless started from a work order
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed a failed start suggesting a retry when the runner's machine had no git credentials; the error now says whom to ask and what to do if the repository is wrong
  • Fixed the self-hosted runner's last_poll_age_seconds reading 0 while the runner had never polled successfully
  • Fixed the notice about a skipped scheduled task that names no organization: it now says to start Claude Code with --resume, because /resume inside a running session doesn't run the task
  • Fixed claude plugin validate wrongly warning that a mod's AbovePrompt or AbovePromptList hook never runs in VS Code
  • Fixed /design-sync deleting a file it had just uploaded when Claude Design stored that file under a changed name
  • Reverted 2.1.329's removal of the automatic retry when max_tokens exceeds a model's or gateway's limit
  • Improved the claude.ai sign-in link shown by /login, claude auth login and claude setup-token: it is now much shorter
  • Windows: Improved Grep and Glob speed by no longer starting a console host for each built-in ripgrep search on a local path
  • Improved the speed of file diffs
  • Improved /config search: most settings whose name starts with what you type come first, "effort" finds Model, and "dark" or "light" finds Theme
  • Improved /resume: sessions where you only opened a screen such as /model and left are no longer listed
  • Improved Reconnect in /mcp and /plugin: a server's page now stays open, with the cause in view, when the server still fails or needs sign-in
  • Improved the error on macOS when sandbox deny lists are too long: it now names the long lists and how to shorten them
  • Improved /plugin in fullscreen mode: the page of a plugin with errors now starts with those errors
  • Improved /ultrareview's cost confirmation on Team and Enterprise plans: it now says how much of your monthly spend limit is left when that is less than a review usually costs
  • Improved self-hosted runner sessions on Amazon Bedrock or Google Cloud's Agent Platform to say so when they start on another default model because your account refused the first
  • Windows: Improved the error when a session's folder is on a drive Claude Code can't verify: it says why, and whether retrying can help
  • Improved Code Mode: Claude is now told how to look at images and PDFs
  • Improved Code Mode: after Esc, "Interrupted" now shows under the stopped command in place of a red error
  • Improved Code Mode: the terminal freezes for far less time after a subagent's script makes thousands of tool calls
  • Changed recurring scheduled tasks and /loop to run up to 30 days instead of 7 while their session keeps running, and say when they end; tasks made before this release still end at 7 days
  • Changed more rm commands aimed at the root, home, a top-level folder or the working folder to ask for approval; where nobody can answer, they're refused
  • Changed deniedMcpServers name entries to hide only the named claude.ai connector, not others at its URL; to block them all, deny its exact URL
  • Changed claude --teleport in some setups to print the git commands for switching branch instead of running them; with -p it exits 1 until you switch
  • Changed unrecognized model names containing "sonnet" or "haiku" to use the shorter system prompt, like other unrecognized names; CLAUDE_CODE_SIMPLE_SYSTEM_PROMPT=0 gives every model the full one
  • Changed skills that Claude runs with a model setting, other than context: fork skills, to leave subagents, forks, compaction and /recap on the session's model

  • Extensible KV cache is on by default: vLLM sizes the KV cache from memory actually free after warmup, so most models get a bigger cache and more throughput - in most cases you should now remove gpu_memory_utilization from your configs.
  • Model Runner V1 is gone. Model Runner V2 is now the only GPU runner.
  • Big speedups on Blackwell and MI355X: up to 1.95× decode (Step5 on GB200), 1.6× throughput (GLM-5.3-Flash), 1.24–1.40× faster long-prompt TTFT (GLM-5.3).
  • Upgrade check: default block size is now 64, ROCm 7.2 images are gone, and huggingface_hub >= 2.0.0 is required. See Before you upgrade.

Highlights

Extensible KV cache, on by default

  • On CUDA and ROCm, the KV cache is sized from memory actually free after CUDA graph capture and warmup, not from an estimate (#56492).
  • Result: a larger cache (e.g. MiniMax-M3 on H200: 433k → 672k tokens), so throughput is higher and TTFT lower at high concurrency.
  • Trade-off: per-token decode latency can rise on some models (TPOT +6–18% on some H200 models at concurrency 128). Opt out with --gpu-memory-utilization 0.9 or --no-enable-extensible-kv-cache.
  • Hardened with fixes for allocator fragmentation, startup OOMs and KV connectors (#67296, #67485, #66731, #66523, #66197, #65137, #66605, #66674).

Model Runner V2 only

  • Model Runner V1 is removed (#63373).
  • Dual-batch overlap now runs on MRV2, including with speculative decoding and DCP (#61464).

Speculative decoding

  • Suffix decoding runs on MRV2 with a GPU speculator; Arctic Inference is no longer needed (#60339).
  • Custom speculators: declarative configs plus a register_speculative_method plugin API (#63205).
  • CUDA graphs for MRV2 draft-model speculators (#60989).
  • Adaptive verification works with XPress (#65175).
  • Draft KV cache matches the target's dtype, so an FP8 target gets an FP8 draft cache (#65198).

  • Model Runner V1 removed (#63373).
    • VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER and VllmConfig.use_v2_model_runner are gone; setting the env var to anything but 1 fails at startup.

    • Deprecated: parallel_drafting, capture_torch_profiler, enable_layerwise_nvtx_tracing.
  • Default --block-size is 64 instead of 16 (#63231). Backends with a preferred block size still override it (ROCm paged attention keeps 16), and an explicit --block-size still wins.
  • gpu_memory_utilization defaults to 1.0 when unset with the extensible KV cache on (#56492). An explicit value in (0.8, 1.0) that withholds 1 GiB or more logs a warning (#66704).
  • ROCm 7.2 wheels and -rocm72 images are no longer published (#61939).
  • Removed:
    • QuTLASS and the fp_quant method (#65230).
    • Marlin INT8/FP8-activation (W4A8) paths and VLLM_MARLIN_INPUT_DTYPE; use --quantization humming with VLLM_HUMMING_INPUT_QUANT_CONFIG (#65542).

  • Model and plugin code: all process_weights_after_loading hooks share one signature and the loader runs every module's hook (#57678); config compute_hash() replaced by compile_factors() / hash_config() (#65652).
  • API behavior:
    • llama3_json no longer streams tool arguments incrementally (#63569).
    • Canary transcription without language returns 400 (#65445).
    • An empty tools array is accepted in both frontends (#65547, #65854).
    • /v1/systemone rejects request-supplied chat templates without --trust-request-chat-template (#64503).

  • New defaults:
